title: Regular Expressions: Search and Parse Text
description: Patterns, captures, flags, and safer text extraction.
learningOutcomes: Build patterns with groups, character classes, quantifiers, and anchors.
Distinguish substring search from whole-string checks.
Extract multiple results safely and explain how g/y affect lastIndex.
Assess regex validation limits and avoid excessively costly patterns.
Escape literal dynamic search text and explain why common format regexes have limited scope.

blocks.text: Regular expressions for searching and processing text

A regular expression describes a pattern in a string; it is not a full grammar or a finished validator. It is useful for extracting, searching, splitting, and checking local formats. First state the rule in words, then decide whether you need a substring search or a whole-string check, and test boundary cases.
Patterns: characters, classes, quantifiers, and groups

steps.title: Turn a requirement into a format
steps.explanation: The ^ and $ anchors require the whole string to match. \s+ separates fields; \d+ requires one or more digits; groups capture level, ID, and action.

steps.title: Read the match and captures
steps.explanation: exec returns null on failure or an array: [0] is the full match and [1..] are captured groups. For a complex grammar, a dedicated parser may be clearer.

steps.title: Check that extra text is rejected
steps.explanation: The added prefix does not match because of the start anchor. Without anchors, a search might find a valid-looking fragment inside an invalid string.

items: g searches for all matches but makes test/exec stateful through lastIndex.
i ignores case; m changes how ^ and $ work on strings containing line breaks.
s lets . match line breaks; u enables Unicode mode. Flags change pattern meaning and should be deliberate.
A /pattern/ literal is convenient for a fixed pattern; new RegExp(text) is useful for dynamic patterns, but dynamic input must be escaped correctly.
`d` adds start/end indices for captured substrings to the match result; it does not change which text matches.
`g` searches repeatedly and advances `lastIndex`; `y` (sticky) only tries to match at `lastIndex` rather than searching forward. Both need deliberate state handling.
`i` ignores case; `m` makes `^`/`$` operate per line; `s` lets `.` match line breaks.
`u` enables Unicode code-point mode. `v` adds Unicode set features and cannot be combined with `u`; use it when the target runtime supports it and its extra class syntax is needed.

blocks.title: A global RegExp is not a pure predicate
blocks.text: With /pattern/g, calls to test() and exec() advance lastIndex. Rechecking the same string can alternate between true and false. Remove g for a boolean check; use matchAll with a global pattern to extract every result, or explicitly reset lastIndex.
Substring or whole string? Search, extract, replace

steps.title: Notice the retained state
steps.explanation: The first test finds 7 and leaves lastIndex after the match; the second search starts there, fails, and resets it. That makes a global pattern dangerous in a repeatedly called predicate.

steps.title: Extract every match and its group
steps.explanation: matchAll yields matches and captured values, preserving match indexes. It requires a global pattern and avoids manually changing the original regex's lastIndex.

blocks.text: Replace using captured data, not only a fixed string

steps.title: Capture only the numeric portion
steps.explanation: The outer group captures the amount; ?: makes the decimal part a non-capturing group so the callback receives only the values it needs.

steps.title: Process each match
steps.explanation: The global flag applies the replacement to both prices; the callback receives the full match and captured amount. Here it converts, multiplies, and formats the value.

steps.title: Inspect the result
steps.explanation: The result is `Items: $11.00, $2.75`; replace returns a new string and leaves the original unchanged.

blocks.text: Practical patterns: extract candidates and state the limits

Common examples include a local phone-number shape, a password policy, URL candidates, hashtags, and whitespace normalization. These patterns implement only the policy written into them: phone formats differ by region, password requirements differ by product, and a URL-matching regex is not a complete URL parser. Explain what a pattern accepts before calling it validation.

steps.title: Write the exact policy in the pattern
steps.explanation: The phone pattern recognizes one illustrative 10-digit arrangement; the password pattern encodes one explicit character/length policy. Neither is a universal international rule, and neither should be the only security boundary.

steps.title: Separate the input from the operations
steps.explanation: The sample contains a phone number, URL, hashtags, and repeated spaces so each example has a concrete input.

steps.title: Test local formats without overclaiming
steps.explanation: test() answers only whether a string matches the chosen expression. It does not confirm a phone number is assigned or a password is secure against every threat.

steps.title: Extract and normalize with explicit limits
steps.explanation: These expressions demonstrate simple URL-candidate extraction, hashtag extraction, and whitespace normalization. The URL example intentionally skips a comma delimiter; it is not a standards-complete URL parser.

blocks.text: Build a RegExp from text without treating text as syntax

steps.title: Escape regex metacharacters in literal input
steps.explanation: If a search phrase comes from a user and should match literally, escape characters such as +, ., *, ?, (, and [ before passing the text to RegExp. Otherwise the input changes the pattern's meaning.

steps.title: Construct the pattern only after escaping
steps.explanation: The constructor receives a string, so the pattern's escaping rules are different from writing a regex literal directly in source code. Keep flags intentional and validate the constructed pattern where input or configuration can vary.

steps.title: Verify literal matching with a metacharacter
steps.explanation: The phrase C++ matches the literal text C++, not a different string such as C. This helper is for literal searches; it does not make arbitrary complex patterns safe from ReDoS.

blocks.prompt: A search box accepts text that should be treated literally, such as `C++`. What is the safest approach before using `new RegExp(text, 'i')`?

options.text: Escape regex metacharacters in the user text before constructing the pattern
options.feedback: Escaping makes characters such as + or . literal instead of allowing user text to change the regex operators.

options.text: Add the global flag so every character becomes literal
options.feedback: The g flag controls repeated matching and lastIndex; it does not escape metacharacters.

options.text: Wrap the input in ^ and $ without escaping it
options.feedback: Anchors require a whole-string match, but unescaped metacharacters still change the constructed pattern.

options.text: Use eval to parse the user's expression as JavaScript
options.feedback: Eval executes JavaScript and is not needed to construct a RegExp; it increases risk instead of escaping the input.

blocks.explanation: The RegExp constructor treats its first argument as pattern syntax. Escape user-provided literal text before constructing a regex; separate regex syntax from a literal search string.

blocks.text: A /^...$/ check answers a question about one specific format. A primitive email pattern cannot establish that an address exists and may reject valid addresses; for ordinary forms, use input type=email and server-side checks based on product requirements. Complex or adversarial patterns with nested ambiguous quantifiers can cause catastrophic backtracking and a hang (ReDoS).

blocks.title: Extract ticket references from a note
blocks.context: Support notes contain references like #123. Return the numeric IDs in order, reject matches inside words such as ticket#123abc, and avoid leaking lastIndex state across calls.
instructions: Implement extractTicketIds(text), returning an array of IDs as strings.
A match must start at the string boundary or after whitespace/punctuation, and end at a boundary rather than inside an alphanumeric token.
Handle multiple references and no matches; explain the global search choice and how repeated calls avoid lastIndex leakage.
Add checks for '#7', 'Fix (#12), then #34', 'ticket#123abc', empty text, and two consecutive calls with different results.
Do not use regex as a substitute for authorization checks or server-side validation.
Add a helper that escapes regex metacharacters before constructing a RegExp from literal search text, and explain why a URL or password pattern is only as strong as its stated requirements.
requirements: Returns all IDs in source order and excludes the # character.
Returns an empty array when there are no matches.
Repeated calls do not depend on lastIndex left by an earlier call.
Input text is not mutated; explanation distinguishes substring extraction from whole-string validation.
Dynamic literal search text is escaped before RegExp construction; practical-format patterns are described as limited examples rather than universal validators.
hints: Consider lookbehind or capture the allowed separator; do not include that separator in the returned ID.
Choose a token boundary so a letter/digit cannot appear before # or continue after the digits.
matchAll is convenient for global capture extraction; create the pattern locally per call or account for lastIndex.
Test the empty result and repeated calls to the same function.
Test a query containing `+`, `.`, or `(`, because these characters have meaning in regex syntax.
successCriteria: Two consecutive calls with different strings return independent correct results.
Implementation excludes #/separators and does not modify the input.
Explains why test with /g may depend on lastIndex.
A dynamic phrase such as `C++` is matched literally; the explanation identifies limits of phone, URL, and password patterns.

blocks.prompt: A function repeatedly calls pattern.test(value), where pattern is /\d+/g. Why can results change for the same value?

options.text: The g flag stores lastIndex between calls, and test advances it.
options.feedback: Correct. Regex state changes; remove g for a predicate or manage lastIndex explicitly.

options.text: The g flag makes digits case-insensitive.
options.feedback: The i flag controls case; g means global matching and affects lastIndex.
The behavior is deterministic and depends on the current lastIndex.
The input string is not mutated; state lives on the RegExp object.

blocks.explanation: A regex with g or y stores a continuation position in lastIndex. test() uses and updates it, so the same instance does not always begin at the start of the string.

blocks.prompt: Why does matching a simple /^...$/ email pattern not prove that an address is deliverable?

options.feedback: Regex can check many string formats, but it cannot prove deliverability.

options.text: A match checks the chosen string shape, not whether the address exists or every valid address rule.
options.feedback: Correct. Use appropriate client-side format checks and a server-side validation/confirmation process.

options.text: Anchors are always forbidden in email checks.
options.feedback: Anchors are useful for whole-string checks; the problem is overclaiming what a simplified pattern proves.

options.text: The i flag guarantees the mail server accepts the address.
options.feedback: i changes case matching, not address existence or delivery.

blocks.explanation: A regular expression is a local pattern matcher. It cannot confirm an inbox exists and should not present a rough approximation as a complete grammar.

items: Anchors check a whole string; without them a search may find a matching fragment inside an invalid value.
Groups capture values; matchAll suits multiple matches, while a replace callback can calculate replacements.
g/y change lastIndex; do not reuse such an instance as a simple test predicate without controlling its state.
Regex is not a substitute for native/server validation; bound pattern complexity to reduce ReDoS risk.
